problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3 \\ 7\end{aligned}],\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector onto the Solution Space of a System of Equations
examples.problem:
Given the vector $\mathbf{x}$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the solution space of the system.
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066555/assets/37beee87c5b5bd6350bd2c0f6353b61b1cfd321449a96b8b66aac99584d459bb.png)
examples.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:    

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are $2$ pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, $x_3$ is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get $x_2=4x_3.$ 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain  

$$
x_1+4x_3+4x_3= 0
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
x_1=-8x_3.
$$

So, the general solution is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066555/assets/4995b9959cbb8a412fe0ed6198bfa9a82bcda40cd388c4759589e060ec16de1e.png)
Consequently, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066555/assets/232c58060c7ba67f66564e8f8667fe67a84f6ef886a1c56e2d042224ace9b4db.png) is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{(-10)\cdot (-8)+20\cdot 4+2\cdot 1}{{(-8)}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{80+80+2}{64+16+1}b \\  & =\frac{162}{81}b \\  & =2b \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-16 \\ 8 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem: Let $x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]$ and $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ If $x=y+z,$ where $y\in \text{Span}{a}$ and $z⊥\text{Span}{a},$ then $z=$
feedback.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066555/assets/d887852fe51f08cb7296437e69b6a9632721cfd155558e6abf9a99b4f59f7ad6.png)

First, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{a}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x & =\frac{a\cdot x}{a\cdot a}a \\  & =\frac{1\cdot 3+2\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 2+3\cdot 4}{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{3}^{2}}a \\  & =\frac{3+2+(-2)+12}{1+4+1+9}a \\  & =\frac{15}{15}a \\  & =a \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={\text{proj}}_{a}\,x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ z & =x-{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $y\in \text{Span}{a}$ and $z⊥\text{Span}{a},$ as shown in the picture above.

In conclusion, $z=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$
